Date: 25-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20055788

Purpose: ChatGPT Administration
Question Asked: The client has recently launched ChatGPT at scale, with approximately 10,000 licenses, and is now focused on driving adoption and operationalizing usage across the organization. While initial rollout is complete, the team is working through administrative and governance considerations, particularly in an environment without API integrations. They are seeking guidance on how to effectively manage, monitor, and expand ChatGPT usage, while identifying high-value use cases and opportunities to integrate into existing workflows.

What are best practices for administering and governing enterprise ChatGPT deployments without API integrations, including reporting and usage tracking?
What integration opportunities exist to embed ChatGPT into workflows when APIs are not currently leveraged?
How are leading organizations driving adoption and identifying high-value use cases at scale?
Analyst Name: Max Goss
Discussion Summary: Response sent: Hi Jennifer,

Nice to meet you. My name is Max Goss, and I'm a senior Analyst that covers Enterprise AI tools including Chat GPT Enterprise. 

Please see below my response to your questions. I'm assuming this is ChatGPT Enterprise (not Business). While both are similar at the feature level, Enterprise has more advanced administration controls.

What are best practices for administering and governing enterprise ChatGPT deployments without API integrations, including reporting and usage tracking?
Govern in layers using the following key areas: identity and access, workspace design, roles and permissions, monitoring and reporting.
Identity and access: enable SCIM directory sync, -limited to the users and groups that will hold a license to create, update and remove accounts and invitations automatically; verify the corporate domain to enforce SSO-only login (not personal subscriptions to GPT) and automatic domain claiming. Due to the use of shadow AI and the lack of early governance controls, some employees may have used their corporate email addresses to sign up for ChatGPT using a personal consumer account.  Before provisioning users into ChatGPT Enterprise, organizations should identify whether employees have already created personal ChatGPT accounts with corporate email addresses. This discovery should include checks with procurement, expense management, and the OpenAI account team to identify existing subscriptions and likely shadow AI usage.  In these situations, OpenAI supports a migration path from Personal accounts to Business or Enterprise licenses. Organize users into groups and use these to control access to certain features.
Workspace design: Start by deciding whether a single workspace or multiple workspaces best fit the organization. A single workspace simplifies the end user experience and avoids fragmentation of chats, GPTs, and ownership. Multiple workspaces can improve billing separation, delegated administration, and adoption reporting, but they also introduce management overhead and can complicate user transitions between groups. If multiple workspaces are used, design them around relatively stable operating boundaries such as billing entities, major business units, or broad usage patterns rather than narrow reporting lines. Reorganizations are common, and ChatGPT Enterprise does not yet provide mature tools to merge or move content cleanly across workspaces. 
Roles and Owners: Define at least two owners per workspace because this role has the broadest authority, including billing and responsibility for assets that may be reassigned automatically, such as GPTs whose original owner leaves the workspace. Assign Admin to IT and security, Analytics Viewer to adoption leads, and leave most users as Members; then use custom roles to disable preview models by default and restrict advanced features — Agent Mode, ChatGPT Record, Atlas, connector creation and external GPT publishing — to champion groups.
Monitoring reporting and analytics: use the User Analytics page to track usage and identify AI power users, native audit logs to record logins, administrative changes and connector activity, and Impact Surveys plus the group usage tab for experience and team-level adoption. These native capabilities are enough to begin, but they are reactive: they show that an event occurred without enforcing policy or remediating, and OpenAI retains compliance data only for a limited period. As such, you will need to think about exporting logs to meet longer term compliance requirements. ChatGPT Enterprise includes a Compliance API that allows organizations to export audit and activity data from the workspace into existing eDiscovery, DLP, and SIEM tools. The API provides time stamped records of user interactions, uploaded files, workspace configuration, and administrative events. Compliance data is retained by OpenAI for a limited period, requiring organizati

Question Asked: Abe is part of the Enterprise Architecture team at Tractor Supply.  As they are leveraging more AI and Agentic AI, Abe would like to discuss AI coding harness.  What are the best practices here?

Update 04/17/2026:
An AI coding harness is the organizational configuration and control layer that sits between an AI coding product (agentic coding platform) and your codebase; it comprises versioned, machine readable artifacts (rules files, coding standards, CLAUDE.md or equivalent), managed settings, enforcement hooks and verification gates that govern how AI agents generate and validate code before it reaches repositories or production.

He shared that Tractor uses a number of coding tools and wanted to understand how best to apply harness to these.

I pulled up insights from C. A. Swan when we were on the call (Software Engineering AI Briefing: Agentic Leaps with Agent Teams and Harnesses and For Agentic SDLC, the AI Coding Harness Matters More Than the Coding Model) and he said these were on point and what he would like to dive deeper into.

Could we align this call with C. A. Swan?

Purpose: AI  travel purchasing behaviors
Question Asked: I’m reaching out because, as part of my current work, I would like to gain insight into the evolution of travel purchasing behaviors related to generative and agentic AI, with a primary focus on the US and Chinese markets (if data is available).

-Fragmentation vs. Package: Does AI encourage end-to-end trip booking (facilitated multimodality), or do purchases remain siloed (booking travel and hotels separately)?
-Preferred interfaces: What types of platforms are attracting audiences (AI-powered native travel apps, generalist chatbots like ChatGPT, or Super-Apps like WeChat/Alipay)?
-From “Conversational” to “Agentic”: Is there a shift from information to action, with delegation of the purchase act?
Analyst Name: Brad Jashinsky
Discussion Summary: I shared consumer insight data on GenAI usage and examples of GenAI use in travel.

We expect that agentic bookings will take many years to gain market share. The technology needs to be worked out first and then the hard part of changing consumer behavior will likely take place over several years. It took 15 years for U.S. consumers to make more ecommerce purchases via mobile devices than computers.

OpenAI announced in March 2026 the end of Instant Checkout and Agentic Checkout. That includes pilots that were being conducted with both OTAs and retailers.

This was due to less consumer demand than OpenAI expected for the feature and higher than expected engineering costs to integrate into travel and retail systems.

That aligns with Gartner’s consumer research which shows that consumers are increasingly using GenAI search tools for discovery but are not comfortable with fully automated purchasing. 

However, consumers, especially U.S. consumers, cite convenience as a top value, making agentic commerce appealing in the long term.

Google continues to experiment with agentic commerce. Google’s UCP documentation hints at travel bookings, but is only currently designed for retailers. The protocol will need to be broadened to support travel bookings. Google has a big advantage of already having partnerships with most travel companies and is already offering agentic restaurant reservations.

Date: 15-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20105994
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: IT - Other Role
Purpose: Written Response: Organizational Decisions to Move Away from Copilot
Question Asked: Chris (Chief of Staff) would like to understand the following:
--What are the primary reasons organizations are choosing to turn off Microsoft Copilot and instead contract with third-party AI solutions (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic), even when Copilot offers seamless integration with Microsoft 365 and similar licensing costs?
--Are there specific challenges, limitations, or concerns (e.g., security, functionality, cost, user experience, data privacy, or other factors) that are driving these decisions?
--What are the observed benefits or drawbacks for organizations that have made this switch?
--Are there any best practices or lessons learned from clients who have evaluated both options?

A written summary addressing these points would be appreciated. If there are relevant case studies, data points, or research notes, please include or reference them.
Analyst Name: Adam Preset
Discussion Summary: The client sought clarity on why some organizations opt to move away from Microsoft Copilot in favor of third-party AI assistants like OpenAI and Anthropic, and what challenges, benefits, and best practices are associated with these decisions. Our advice was direct: it is rare for organizations to fully disable Microsoft Copilot Chat, as its inclusion in Microsoft 365, ease of deployment, and mature data governance make it a practical, cost-effective everyday AI solution for most users.
When organizations do pursue alternatives, the drivers are usually leadership vision, unique use case requirements, or the desire for strategic partnerships, not cost or integration issues. Key challenges with third-party tools include less mature data governance, different user experiences, and the need for separate administration. While ChatGPT and Anthropic are sometimes viewed as more creative or accessible, Microsoft Copilot is more business-focused and leverages both OpenAI and Anthropic models depending on the service. Costs across these solutions are broadly similar.
There is no evidence of widespread, clear benefits or drawbacks from switching entirely to third-party AI assistants. Instead, most organizations maintain a multi-tool strategy: Copilot Chat for all users and additional tools for targeted roles or use cases. This approach supports cross-validation, user preferences, and avoids overdependence on a single vendor.
Best practices include segmenting users, requiring business-led justification for exceptions, and ongoing measurement of adoption and impact. A layered AI strategy (everyday AI, role-specific AI, low-code/no-code, and platform AI) is recommended. IT should support, but not own, the business case for exceptions. Organizations should be cautious about overcommitting to tools in beta and prioritize generally available, vendor-supported offerings.
#value Delivered practical, research-backed guidance that clarified the rarity of full Copilot replacement, shifted the client’s thinking toward a multi-tool, layered AI strategy, and provided actionable best practices for governance and adoption.
#AIvalue Provided a structured framework for evaluating, segmenting, and deploying enterprise AI assistants, with emphasis on business-led justification and ongoing measurement.

Date: 17-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19429455
Buyer Region: EMEA
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: IT - Other Role
Purpose: AI Literacy Programs - BBVA
Question Asked: Dear RES,

My client:

I just finished a session with Madelin Santana about AI Literacy Programs and we chatted (selfie included, haha) about how her presentation fits with our training journey. We arranged to schedule an inquiry to get more information.

Could you please send the link for this call with Madelin?
Analyst Name: Madelin Santana
Discussion Summary: La conversación se centró en la estrategia de despliegue de herramientas de IA generativa en BBVA y los factores clave para impulsar su adopción a escala.
Estrategia de despliegue
BBVA inició su adopción de IA generativa con aproximadamente 3.000 licencias de ChatGPT, evaluando su impacto y casos de uso dentro de la organización. Paralelamente, se analizaron las ventajas de distintas plataformas, incluyendo Google Gemini y ChatGPT, considerando aspectos tecnológicos, de adopción y alineación con las necesidades del negocio.
Actualmente, el banco cuenta con una estrategia dual:

120.000 empleados del Grupo con acceso a Gemini.
Acuerdo con OpenAI para extender el acceso a ChatGPT a otros 120.000 empleados a nivel global.

El objetivo no ha sido únicamente tecnológico, sino también impulsar un salto cultural que permita integrar la IA en la forma de trabajar de la organización. Tras los primeros despliegues, la iniciativa se extendió a áreas como Servicios Centrales y otras funciones corporativas.
Casos de uso y adopción
Aunque se han identificado múltiples casos de éxito, el principal desafío no ha sido la tecnología, sino la adopción. Aproximadamente un 15% de las licencias activadas no mostraron uso efectivo, lo que evidenció la necesidad de trabajar sobre el cambio de comportamiento y no solo sobre la disponibilidad de las herramientas.
El enfoque de adopción se ha centrado en:

Generar entusiasmo sobre las oportunidades de la IA.
Gestionar los miedos y percepciones de amenaza asociados al cambio.
Apoyarse inicialmente en una masa crítica reducida de early adopters que actúan como referentes para el resto de la organización.

Gestión de la resistencia al cambio
Para abordar la resistencia, BBVA implementó varias prácticas:

Escuchar y entender las barreras reales mediante encuestas de pulso (pulse surveys) para identificar patrones de uso, fricciones y elementos que no estaban funcionando.
Crear una red de apoyo y evangelización, compuesta por:

Master Champions.
Champions de negocio.
"Wizards" o usuarios avanzados que participaron en pilotos.
Equipos responsables de infraestructura, arquitectura y despliegue.



Esta comunidad se convirtió en un mecanismo clave para acelerar la adopción y compartir mejores prácticas.
Formación y cultura de IA
La organización ha acompañado el despliegue con un programa continuo de capacitación y comunicación interna, incluyendo:

Planes formativos.
Tips prácticos de uso.
Newsletters.
Webinars y sesiones informativas.
Encuestas periódicas sobre cultura de IA, como la iniciativa mostrada en Ingeniería España.

El aprendizaje principal es que el éxito de la IA generativa depende menos de la tecnología y más de la capacidad de la organización para construir una cultura de adopción, desarrollar confianza en las herramientas y crear comunidades que faciliten el cambio de comportamiento a gran escala.

1. Shift from Tool Adoption to Value Adoption
The current focus appears to be measuring activations and usage. The next step is measuring business outcomes.
Key actions:

Define the top 10-15 use cases by function.
Track productivity gains, time saved, quality improvements, and employee satisfaction.
Create a "Value Dashboard" that shows business impact rather than number of prompts or licenses activated.

2. 2. Expand the Champion Network into Communities of Practice
The Master Champions, Champions, and Wizards are a strong foundation.
Next evolution:

Create AI Communities by function (Engineering, Risk, HR, Marketing, Operations).
Host monthly "AI Wins" sessions where employees showcase successful use cases.
Build an internal repository of prompts, workflows, and success stories.

3. Segment Adoption Strategies
Not all employees resist for the same reasons.

Of course, they are an implementer, and so they have a mindset regarding "best solutions are those we deliver". However, I think the team at Deutsche Post will have a similar "implementer" mindset that permits discerning the professional services preferences from the functional advantages.

Microsoft Fabric Roadmap
Microsoft Fabric’s strategic planning indicates a convergence of data management technologies into unified ecosystems by 2028—enabled by the data fabric architecture and GenAI. It further highlights that by 2027, a significant majority (80%) of new analytics workloads will rely on open table formats (Gartner: 825688, Gartner: 766737). This roadmap emphasizes:

Continued Integration of GenAI: With tools like Copilot increasingly embedded in Fabric, Microsoft aims to transform data interaction and report generation.
Evolution of Self-Service Analytics: Emphasizing frameworks such as the self-service analytics reference architecture and the migration away from legacy Power BI Premium capacities.
Focus on Governance and Compliance: Strengthening data governance and metadata management through internal catalogs and Microsoft Purview integration.
The roadmap reflects a commitment to reducing technology complexity by converging disparate data management tools. However, the deep integration with the Microsoft ecosystem may limit flexibility for organizations seeking multi-cloud or cross-platform solutions.

Databricks Roadmap and Strategic Partnerships
In contrast, Databricks is leveraging its recent strategic partnerships to redefine its platform as a model-independent data + AI + agents hub. Its roadmap, signified by dual partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI, along with heavy investments in agentic systems (e.g., Agent Bricks, Databricks One), targets the following objectives:

Enhanced AI Agent Capabilities: By integrating Claude 3 and GPT-5 models natively into its platform, Databricks is enabling enterprises to perform complex reasoning on governed data without massive data movement.
Model Neutrality and Cloud Agnosticism: Databricks is positioning itself as a neutral intermediary that can serve enterprises with multi-cloud strategies and reduce vendor lock-in.
Expanding Beyond Data Infrastructure: The platform now addresses the entire lifecycle of AI application development, from data ingestion and processing to AI model execution and governance (Gartner: 842579, Gartner: 842640).
Databricks’ strategic investments are reflected in its partnerships and product announcements—recently including a $100 million multiyear agreement with OpenAI and a five-year integration with Anthropic’s models. These alliances aim to bolster its AI capabilities, addressing both the financial and operational challenges that arise with such high-end integrations. The roadmap suggests that the company is not only current with trends but is also dedicated to leading in agentic AI and orchestration—a field that is increasingly relevant for self-service analytics, where users demand smart, adaptive systems (Gartner: 842579).

Discussion Summary: Key Recommendations & Attached Research Context
1. Moving to Outcome-Based Performance (Focus: Accuracy & Experience)
Traditional "uptime" SLAs are insufficient for AI. We need to hold TechM accountable for the quality of the AI’s decisions.

Recommendation: Include "Accuracy Warranties" (e.g., the 90% threshold mentioned in their proposal) and Experience-Level Agreements (XLAs) to ensure the system is actually providing value to your complaint handlers.


Attached Note: Tool: How to Measure AI Agents. This note provides a framework for transitioning from traditional metrics to those focused on agent performance, reliability, and business alignment.  

2. Implementing "Carrot and Stick" Commercials
Given the high ROI targets ($65 down to $43 per complaint), we should share the risk and the reward.

Recommendation: Stagger payments contingent on meeting both technical and business outcome milestones. I suggest a 5% penalty per missed high-value SLA, balanced by an "incentive" or revenue-sharing component if they measurably exceed performance targets (e.g., getting costs down to $35).


Attached Note: How to Structure Penalties and Incentives for Outsourcing Deals. Use this to define measurable behavior drivers and financial "Amount at Risk" (AaR) to ensure vendor accountability.  

3. Codifying AI Governance and RACI
With "Human-in-the-Loop" being critical to your regulatory compliance, the division of labor between your team and the AI must be ironclad.

Recommendation: Demand a detailed RACI chart in the SOW that explicitly specifies whether a human or the AI system is responsible for executing, validating, or approving each task.


Attached Note: AI-Enabled IT Services: A Framework for Operational Excellence. This research includes a sample "AI-Augmented RACI" that illustrates how roles must adapt across the project life cycle.

        Thank you for your inquiry.  The following is the response to your questions:

What are the new software development methodologies that can be integrated into our application strategy?
The use of AI coding agents and agentic AI across the software development lifecycle (SDLC) has increased the throughput of software creation. AI coding agents such as Cursor, Windsurf, Google Antigravity, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex have been used to great effect to accelerate code writing. Additionally, code review agents have been implemented to address the bottleneck that occurs after coding. These agents, used in tandem with human reviews, help ensure that we do not incur an excessive amount of technical debt from using AI coding assistance. Beyond AI coding agents and code review, companies are also seeing great success using AI for testing. They leverage epics, features, stories, and acceptance criteria, as well as specification-driven development, to create tests and generate test scripts for tools like Selenium. Furthermore, clients are utilizing AI to assist in the creation of epics, features, and stories, and to collaborate with developers and product personnel on specification development. Tools like Atlassian’s JIRA now include Rovo, which can be used to decompose requirements from sources such as requirements databases or call transcripts, and to break down epics, features, stories, and their acceptance criteria. Tools like AgentOS and specification-driven development platforms such as Github Spec Kit and AWS’s Kiro have also been leveraged to create highly specific and detailed prompts in markdown files, which can be used by AI coding tools to generate feature software.
How can AI be utilized to speed up the process from analysis documentation to product development?
As mentioned in the answer to question one, AI can be utilized to accelerate the process from analysis documentation to product development through the use of AI coding agents. The CBRE case study is a great example of how agentic AI is leveraged in the SDLC. CBRE created agents to help generate epics, features, and stories based on requirements databases. They also developed agents to assist with testing and documentation. See this case study in the attached documentation. Additionally, companies like Revvity are using agentic AI to create code in a nearly frictionless SDLC. Refer to the attached documentation for more information on the zero-friction SDLC.
What alternatives should we consider to support our current and future projects?
To support your current and future projects, you should first consider a robust agentic coding tool. Tools that are prevalent in the marketplace now include Microsoft’s GitHub Copilot, Anthropic’s Claude Code, and Cursor. Leverage these tools to accelerate your software creation. Beyond that, review your existing SDLC tools to see how you can integrate agentic and assistive generative AI technologies. For example, use Rovo within Atlassian, the AI plugin inside Azure DevOps, or natural language processing to design in Figma or Adobe. You can also utilize the newly created design function in Anthropic’s Claude.

Are there any new use cases, or industry shifts worth highlighting from this perspective?
Analyst Name: Satish Gopalghare
Discussion Summary: The enterprise AI agent framework landscape is evolving rapidly, with a shift from basic construction to operational controls like observability, governance, and cost management. Next-generation frameworks emphasize persistent memory, multiagent orchestration, and domain-specialized models to optimize performance and cost. Standards now require runtime controls, modular architectures, and embedded governance for scaling. Top use cases include customer service automation, knowledge management, cybersecurity, coding, finance, and industry-specific workflows. Industry shifts highlight the move from LLM assistants to agentic architectures, increased focus on data governance, and rising security challenges due to agent sprawl.

Date: 18-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20112505
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: Deputy Technology Leader or Office of CIO
Purpose: Government Tenets for AI
Question Asked: Do Anthropic and OpenAI have any government tenet licenses available at the enterprise level? If not, have we heard anything about possible releases on these in the future? Lastly, outside of Copilot, are there any other largely available AI model vendors that do have government tenet licensing available?
Analyst Name: Michael Berkholtz
Discussion Summary: In addition to Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are offering enterprise licenses. Note that many enterprise licenses now are starting to add on usage-based pricing above a certain tier.

Government licensing is being offered by the major providers as evidenced by the number of vendors negotiating with the US General Services Administration under the OneGov initiative (OneGov IT | IT Vendor Management Office). While most of these pricing agreements under the OneGov are only available to federal agencies, the license and purchase types are being provided through government services. Anthropic, OpenAI, Perplexity and xAI, as well as Microsoft and Google are offering enterprise license type pricing through this arrangement. AWS is also offering access to their tools through their marketplace under enterprise licenses, but pricing is variable and dictated by usage. Based on conversations with clients and former colleagues in the federal government, these agreements and pricing models are expected to evolve.

Generally pricing models with any of the AI models and providers are still very fluid. This is primarily due to the evolving nature of generative AI, LLMs and costs associated with training, maintaining, and updating/upgrading these models. LLM providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI are constantly building and retiring their LLMs so availability of these products are changing. Commercial providers still have not yet figured out their own internal costs to develop, maintain, and support models. As model functionality is being more clearly understood and explainable and value creating use cases are being expanded, vendors will be better able to account for the true costs of their products and then begin settling around pricing models. 

As the research below will show, this is very much a work in progress. Even enterprise license deals for ‘seats’ are seeing added surcharges for usage above a certain threshold.

Analyst Name: Paulo Aresta
Discussion Summary: •	Meeting Focus and Context:
o	The discussion centered on DLP, specifically around the challenges of users emailing company information to personal email addresses and using ChatGPT outside approved channels.
o	The organization is a Microsoft shop (E3 + E5 Security), uses Purview for DLP and also leverages Zscaler for data protection.
•	Current DLP Challenges:
o	Users bypassing controls by sending data to personal emails and then using external AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) before returning information to corporate channels.
o	DLP is currently reactive, with investigations uncovering policy violations after the fact.
o	The organization is seeking to move toward a more proactive DLP posture and avoid common pitfalls.
•	Personal Email Use Case:
o	While some personal email usage (e.g., sharing payslips or tax documents) may be legitimate, company-sensitive information should not be allowed to leave via personal domains.
o	Contractors should only access sensitive data through company infrastructure (e.g., SharePoint, OneDrive), where MFA is enforced, not personal email.
o	Blocking all outbound to personal emails and managing exceptions manually is not sustainable long-term.
•	Best Practices and Recommendations:
o	Paulo recommends starting with monitor policies to understand data flows and build simple dashboards/reports to identify high-risk behaviors and domains.
o	Engage business units with real data to validate which domains should be blocked or allowed, moving from assumptions to evidence-based policy.
o	Technology is evolving: modern DLP solutions now incorporate user behavior analytics, risk scoring, and AI-driven context for more predictive and adaptive controls.
•	Purview and Microsoft Ecosystem Limitations:
o	Purview works best within the Microsoft ecosystem; coverage and automation are limited with E3 licenses and outside Microsoft environments.
o	Purview struggles with non-Office file types (PDFs, CAD, videos, images, source code), leading organizations to supplement it with other DLP or CASB tools.
o	False positives are common, especially with out-of-the-box identifiers (e.g., 9-digit numbers could match many non-sensitive items); customization is recommended.
•	Market Landscape and Alternative Solutions:
o	Zscaler is expanding its data security offerings, now covering endpoints and cloud, and can augment Microsoft Purview for broader coverage.
o	Other notable DLP vendors include Palo Alto, Netskope, Forcepoint, Proofpoint, Fortra (Digital Guardian), Cyberhaven (data lineage) and Jazz Security (LLM/AI-based DLP).
o	Jazz Security allows policy creation via prompts, simplifying DLP management and reporting using AI.
o	The DLP market is evolving rapidly, with mergers, acquisitions and new AI-driven solutions emerging.
•	Data Classification as a Foundation:
o	Data classification is foundational for effective DLP, enabling tailored security controls and visibility.
o	Many organizations lack consistent classification; DLP is possible without it, but classification enhances effectiveness.
o	Recommendations include user training and awareness, enforcing classification standards, and incrementally introducing mandatory classification.

It was a pleasure speaking with you today about the market for enterprise AI search and Glean.

As we discussed, there are several options for adding intelligence to enterprise information:

1.	Approach 1 – in-application search and AI assistants like M365 Search/Copilot and Google Gemini provide search experiences for application suites where work is done. They indexe information in the primary application as well as secondary applications connected to the primary application’s graph. Ie. Microsoft Copilot Connectors

2.	Approach 2 – enterprise AI assistants - connects multiple content and data sources, brokering queries and unifying ranking results from the separate indexes. Enterprise AI assistants are led by LLM vendors like Anthropic, Claude and OpenAI with ChatGPT and Google with Gemini, and integrate with back-end information via MCP or A2A.

3.	Approach 3 – enterprise AI search - connects to multiple content and data sources, enriching a single index to provide a search and AI assistant experience tailored to the needs of specific domains and operational business teams. This is Glean’s approach.

Approach 1 & 2 will be attractive to smaller companies with fewer IT professionals. Approach 3 will be attractive to large organizations and where enterprise applications lack search features or the ability to service MCP requests.

Date: 20-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19478174
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Energy and Utilities
Buyer Role: IT/Cyber Security and Risk Management - Other Role
Purpose: Purview Best Practices in Securing AI
Question Asked: Michael Marshall is seeking to understand how to effectively use Purview to manage sensitive information, identify key data, and ensure proper access controls. He wants to ensure that sensitive data is protected and that AI tools are used securely without exposing critical information. 
Questions are - How can we identify the most sensitive information using Purview? What protections should be in place when integrating AI tools with our data systems? How can we ensure that access management is robust enough to prevent unauthorized data access?
Analyst Name: Paulo Aresta
Discussion Summary: •	Michael described a fast-moving transition from experimenting with Copilot to forming a dedicated AI group and adopting ChatGPT Enterprise. This rapid pace has created significant security concerns, particularly around data protection.
•	Michael’s organization is a Microsoft shop with Purview already implemented (primarily E5 licenses). Purview is seen as the logical first step for data security, but its limitations are acknowledged.
•	Purview offers four main capabilities: data discovery, data classification, DLP (Data Loss Prevention), and insider threat management. Paulo recommended focusing on the first three, cautioning against starting with insider threat due to alert fatigue and lack of prioritization.
•	Out-of-the-box data classification in Purview often requires customization, especially for industry-specific identifiers.
•	Purview’s effectiveness is highest within the Microsoft ecosystem (Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams), but less so for non-Windows environment and non-office file types.
•	Paulo emphasized prioritizing protection of the most sensitive data, rather than attempting to secure everything equally.
•	A phased deployment is recommended, starting with critical business units or repositories.
•	Role-based access controls should leverage existing roles, with manual review steps to ensure accuracy.
•	Michael’s team is small, and alert fatigue is a concern. There is a need for meaningful, actionable alerts, not just volume.
•	Purview alone may not fully mitigate risks associated with GenAI tools like ChatGPT Enterprise, particularly in scenarios where AI can expose data users didn’t know they had access to.
•	Gartner research suggests ChatGPT Enterprise may not always respect Purview data access limitations.
•	Paulo recommended considering Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) tools (e.g., Varonis, Cyera, BigID, Concentric) as complementary solutions for deeper automation, context, and risk mitigation, especially for non-Microsoft file types and advanced insider threat detection.
•	A pilot with Purview is advised to assess coverage and gaps before investing in third-party solutions.

Analyst Name: Whit Andrews
Discussion Summary: Hello Aseem Sinha,

Please accept my apology in advance for relying on dictation and artificial intelligence to help combine several sets of survey data for this response. The analysis draws on how organizations report AI spending both as a percentage of revenue and as absolute dollar figures, as well as how that spending is distributed across different categories. I recognize that this approach requires care in interpretation, particularly given the size and complexity of your business.

Here is research relevant to the conclusions I drew for this letter.

A Strategic Guide to Maturing AI
 

Design an AI Portfolio to Achieve Valued Outcomes
 

Are You Spending Too Much on AI? Here Are Answers In $s and %s
 

How to Decide Whether to Build, Buy or Blend Your AI Projects
 

AI’s Elusive ROI: How to Track, Manage, and Demonstrate the ROI of AI Investments
 

Ten AI Value Metrics for Cost Reduction, Revenue Growth and Productivity
Because of the nature of your organization — an extremely large revenue base combined with unusually dynamic market conditions in this particular year — I want to approach any conclusions with more caution than I might normally apply. This is not a case where headline benchmarks should be taken at face value, nor where proportional comparisons to smaller firms should drive decisions wholesale.

Organizations at your scale generally spend much less as a percentage of revenue than large enterprises. There are sound structural reasons for that. Global enterprises typically operate with highly optimized ecosystems that are already delivering value; they are not usually attempting wholesale reinvention in the way that a smaller large enterprise might, nor can they sustain the same proportional technology spending without distorting capital priorities.

In that context, a total AI spend of approximately $100 million annually places you at the lower end of observed global‑enterprise spending, but still within a reasonable and defensible range — particularly given current market pressures. The more consequential question, therefore, is not simply whether that level of spend is appropriate, but how that spend is distributed.

When we look specifically at global‑enterprise peers, spending tends to fall into three broad categories:

AI platforms and sourcing (including model access and vendor partnerships),
Data and engineering foundations, and
Governance, trust, risk, and security management (TRiSM).
At global‑enterprise scale, organizations typically allocate just over half of their AI spend to platforms and sourcing, approximately one‑third to data foundations, and the remainder to governance and risk capabilities. Applied to a $100M total budget, that implies:

$50–60M toward platforms and model access,
$30–35M toward data, integration, and enablement,
And $15–20M toward governance, trust, risk, and security.
I would stress that the governance component is not discretionary at this level. As AI use scales, under‑investment in trust, risk, and security mechanisms tends to slow deployment, increase internal friction, and ultimately erode leadership confidence in results.

I also want to emphasize something that matters particularly for an organization like yours: clarity about what “value” means at this stage. Organizations that prioritize cost reduction and productivity tend to see more consistent, repeatable returns than those focused primarily on differentiation or transformation. That does not make differentiation or transformation inappropriate — particularly in your industry, where those equations already look very different — but it does mean the success rates are lower, timelines are longer, and expectations must be set deliberately.

To add a bit more color, we also looked at how global enterprises distribute AI spending across business objectives and enterprise functions. I offer this not as prescriptive guidan

Adam advised that most organizations do not license multiple advanced AI tools for all users, but instead provide a core tool and selectively add others where clear business cases exist.
Adam recommended a structured evaluation process for new tools: test use cases, assess unique value, consider cost and support, and weigh productivity and political impacts. He stressed the importance of tracking quantitative usage, qualitative feedback, financial data (including switching costs), and strategic impact (lighthouse stories). The client was advised to require business stakeholders to justify exceptions and avoid redundant tool rollouts unless defensible value is proven.
Adam provided links to essential Gartner research, toolkits, and dashboards to support evaluation and governance. He restated that differentiation among AI vendors is rapidly dissolving, and the decision to add new tools should be driven by strategic goals, executive sponsorship, proven business cases, and readiness to share success stories.
#value The Michael J. Fox Foundation received a clear framework for evaluating AI tool expansion, practical guidance on governance and adoption, and actionable steps to align tool investments with strategic goals. Their thinking advanced from considering broad tool adoption to focusing on targeted, value-driven deployment.

o	Paulo’s guidance emphasized:

•	is it worth committing to a higher quantity now and securing highly discounted pricing for Copilot for the next 3 to 4 years?

•	Where does Gartner see the potential all-time low for AI Assistant cost?
This is a bit time sensitive and we need the call within the next 5 working days.
Analyst Name: Will Sommer
Discussion Summary: Provider token cost trends are being influenced by four main dynamics:

1.	Foundational Model token cost economics are rapidly improving. Holding model scale and design constant, we forecast provider costs will drop by over 90% between 2025-2030.
2.	Better token economics facilitate the commoditization and absorption of relatively simple, generic intelligence. Basic AI features will become table-stakes widely available in open-weight models and productivity software, challenging long-term monetization of these features. You’re already starting to see this with Microsoft embedding some copilot functions in its enterprise license. 
3.	Greater token efficiency is enabling development of significantly more powerful models for higher value use cases. These models require more expensive tokens because larger, more complex models require more computational power to operate.
4.	More complex models and workflows require more tokens. Advanced agentic solutions that can reason require 5-30x more tokens than a basic chatbot performing the same task.  These agents are autonomous and can trigger other agents, resulting in exponentially more token consumption than would be possible by a human using a basic chatbot.
A final dynamic worth mentioning is that prices are currently being subsidized by providers and as AI economics improve, some of those cost savings will be absorbed by vendor margins.
There are of course other macro dynamics here in play like energy prices and interest rates, but even in our scenario analyses where we represent extreme shifts in macro conditions, the effects on AI token costs are relatively muted barring actual scarcity of core AI inputs. 
So what does this all mean?
Inference costs will inevitably go up, but the distribution of cost increases will be uneven.
Monetization for providers will become a treadmill where they will be repacking and repricing commodity features, maybe within enterprise seats, maybe within value-based pricing offerings, while trying to push customers across the chasm toward more expensive agentic capabilities and workflows.
So any questions here around these market fundamentals before we move on to what this all means to Trelleborg?

How does Gartner see/predicts the cost trend for AI Assistants (Copilot, Claude Cowork, Chat GPT, etc.):
•	So the short answer is your AI assistant costs will go up, but there’s some nuance here. If you continue to use AI exactly the same way you do today, with exactly the same model and number of users, your costs will decline precipitously, they may even be completely absorbed into your productivity software licenses. The rub is, you aren’t going to just use the same model for the next 5 years with the same user base. The promise of GenAI is in scaled autonomous work. Your organization will continue to deploy new models against more challenging workflows across more business functions. Each new layer of sophistication will mean an order of magnitude more tokens. 
•	Some of these cost increases will be offset or arbitraged within your existing software licenses, much of it won’t. The actual rate of cost increase will be context specific, I can’t give you a number, but we can talk through some strategies for managing costs if you’d like
•	is it worth committing to a higher quantity now and securing highly discounted pricing for Copilot for the next 3 to 4 years?
•	I can’t speak to the exact circumstances of your business and needs, but we do generally advise against vendor lock-in. And that’s for a number of reasons, but with a vendor like Microsoft basically you’re losing optionality and potentially locking into a generation of models or ecosystem that won’t be best-in-class or even relevant in 3-4 years. The environment is still evolving rapidly and its unclear what providers will ultimately produce the most competitive ecosystems, particularly as they relate to your business needs.

Discussion Summary: Meeting Summary: Caribou Biosciences Data & Integration Strategy
Current State & Workflow Challenges:
Manual Data Handling: The team currently relies on manual workflows, downloading CSV files from lab instruments like bioreactors, HPLCs, and cell counters, and then massaging the data in Excel
.
System Integration: Massaged data is eventually pushed into downstream tools such as Benchling, JMP, SharePoint, and ChatGPT Enterprise
.
Resource Constraints: Integrating these systems is proving tricky, relying on Ignite for storage, and is further complicated because Caribou lacks a dedicated internal data team
.
Key Objectives:
Timeline Reduction: A primary goal is to significantly shorten the current 2-to-3-week timelines for critical processes, such as dosage determination tech transfers and experiments
.
Workflow Visualization: The team needs to move away from building spreadsheet-based workflows for each individual experiment and instead map out visual workflow data structures
.
Strategic Takeaways & Recommended Actions:
Establish Upfront Data Modeling: Shifting away from ad-hoc, "Excel sheet by Excel sheet" transformations requires upfront data modeling to create an agreed-upon, standardized representation of your scientific data. Defining this model ensures that the diverse outputs from your bioreactors, HPLCs, and cell counters share a consistent structure and language before they are analyzed.
Centralize Data Standardization: Instead of manually downloading CSVs and massaging the data within Excel workflows, you should rely on a modern data lake or lakehouse architecture. In this setup, data processing steps—such as standardization, quality control, and aggregation—are handled centrally and systematically in designated processing zones, moving the transformation logic out of fragile spreadsheets.
Utilize Data Hubs or Data Fabrics for Mediation: To automate these standardized transformations and route the data seamlessly, adopt a data hub or a platform equipped with an underlying data fabric. This architecture acts as a central point of mediation, connecting your instrument data directly to tools like Benchling and JMP. It eliminates interface sprawl and removes the need for scientists to act as manual integration points between systems.
Accelerate Experiment Timelines: By mapping out these visual workflows and replacing manual spreadsheet manipulations with a common data model, you will eliminate the primary bottlenecks in your data preparation. Standardizing these specific operational data flows directly supports your goal of significantly shortening the 2-to-3-week timelines for critical processes, such as dosage determination tech transfers and experiments.

Date: 4-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20105148
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Retail
Buyer Role: IT - Other Role
Purpose: Written Response -  ChatGPT for Clinicians Forces Urgent AI Enablement
Question Asked: Client read this new first take + asked for specific insights into how pharmacists may be accessing/utilizing these new LLMs.  I have spoken with Faith Adams and she is able to do a WR for me on this request.  She said that you could schedule this WR over a writing block. 

Document read by client:  G00855070
Analyst Name: Faith Adams
Discussion Summary: Hi Heather 

Here is my written response for Kevin @ Walmart.
Pharmacists are beginning to access and utilize LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and similar AI tools in several ways. And even when not offered by the facility, they may use on their own, creating a shadow AI environment which may create some risks. These tools are often used to augment what a pharmacist may know — using it for information retrieval, patient education and support, and more. 
Common uses:
Research and information: Pharmacists and staff can look up information, check interactions, validate side effects, recheck dosing guidelines, see if new information exists or if there are new publications. They may also use LLMs to summarize studies, look at clinical trial data and insights and more. 
Create patient-friendly education and comms: These solutions can help generate more customer-friendly, plain language information about drugs, managing a disease, how to take meds and more. They can also assist in translations. Some may deploy patient-facing chatbots, too, for consumer Q&A, to augment pharmacists and staff. 
Clinical decision support: They can help draft clinical notes, medication therapy management plans, or suggest potential interventions based on patient data (though always reviewed by the pharmacist). 
Interaction checks/lookups: They can assist in identifying potential interactions. That said, some studies suggest model performance varies for med-related tasks (like this not yet peer-reviewed study).
EX and efficiency: They can help automate routine processes like documentation, reducing admin burden and allowing more face time with customers. (Note: Sometimes pharmacists may use the “shadow tools” due to an unmet workflow need, too, so that is something to consider)
Concerns do exist, like patient privacy and security. Patient data should never be entered in a public LLM, but accidents can happen. In addition, there is the risk of hallucinations and misinformation being provided by LLMs. Clearly, there are risks to the pharmacist here if they use these tools, but there are also risks to patients using these LLMs, too, in place of asking a pharmacist for information (they may get wrong information, outdated information, it may not consider the other meds they are on and more). This can also increase adverse events.

To balance innovation with security, healthcare organizations require a structured approach to AI governance with 
A human-in-the loop for verification to ensure that all AI tools act as assistance tool with a licensed pharmacist always reviewing, verifying, and overriding automated outputs before they impact patient care. Sometimes the information provided by these solutions can be outdated, for example. There is also the risk of information being completely inaccurate.
More of an enterprise deployment: There is a need for a closed-environment LLMs that do not use proprietary data to train the models, etc. (these deployments provide more trust). 

Factors like AI literacy also will matter, too, for pharmacists and staff. Sometimes they may not even think much of the risk of using shadow AI, for example. There is a need for employee education, AI governance and more. I had seen this information about MEDIC (Stanford’s Medication Direction Copilot). But even with something like this, the human in the loop, trusted environment and more are critical. 

I wanted to share this research, too. It is important to consider the various stakeholders with these tools — patients/customers, employees, HCPs, etc. They can indeed be used safely and provide value but it does require thinking about things with HCLS TX in mind.

Date: 13-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19429684
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: Other - Investors
Purpose: Invest - PSP - CSPs / Hyland
Question Asked: Need a call with Tim Nelms on content services platforms & Hyland.  Looking for an update on the current landscape, market trends, competitive dynamics.
Analyst Name: Tim Nelms
Discussion Summary: It was a pleasure speaking with you today about the market for document management platforms (formerly content service platforms).

As we discussed, the Magic Quadrant for Document Management / Critical Capabilities for Document Management give a relatively up-to-date view of the market, however, look out for the new 20206 edition of the MQ for DM, which lands in May. 

The Document Management Platform (DMP) market is substantial, valued at $17.1 billion in 2024, and is projected to expand to $26 billion by 2028, reflecting a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 8.8% (see Forecast: Enterprise Application Software, Worldwide, 2023-2029, 4Q25) for creating, capturing, storing, processing, and delivering enterprise content and unstructured data.

DMPs serve a wide range of collaborative and operational use cases with vendors traditionally performing well at one, but not both experience categories:

•	Collaborative experiences that support the digital workplace, external collaboration, and knowledge management (KM). They enable employees to share content and collaborate, keeping information synchronized across various devices.
•	Operational experiences which facilitate content-centric business processes, enterprise applications, and information governance. They are critical for operational teams across finance, legal, HR, sales, marketing, and R&D.

As a mature market, with many vendors active for over two decades, change is often gradual rather than revolutionary. Across the last 18 months all DMP vendors have changed in response to three key market trends in deployment, AI and experience.
Deployment 
Clients want simpler acquisition, deployment and access to innovation like AI. As a result, two deployment models account for the majority of new purchases. Self-service SaaS is common for collaborative use cases like digital workplace and external collaboration. Vendor-managed services are common for operational use cases. However, there is a growing trend toward SaaS for operational experiences as well. 

SaaS solutions exceeded 50% market share in 2024 and continue to grow at a higher rate than other deployment models. 
AI
Clients deploying AI are investing in AI technology with a focus on democratising access to AI assistants and agents with Microsoft 365 Copilot, Google Gemini, openAI ChatGPT, and Anthropic Claude. Clients who pursue this strategy quickly start to encounter challenges with broad adoption, governance, and return on investment.

The value of content is realised more quickly when curated and exposed by AI, which justifies investments in document management. (See Evaluating AI for Document Management).
Experience 
The number of content experiences is expanding, becoming increasingly nuanced and tuned to operational business needs. Some document management vendors offer prepackaged applications or templates that solve common departmental or industry needs. These solutions may compete with more specific content service applications in markets like engineering document management, contract life cycle management, legal document management and digital asset management. 

Choosing a document management tool has never been more challenging as platforms and applications increasingly vie for attention. (See Content Services Strategy: Through the Lens of Total Experience).

Discussion Summary: Meeting Summary

We discussed the evolving landscape of AI adoption in software development, focusing on the limitations of legacy tools like Windsurf, the rise of agentic SDLC platforms, and the challenges of building trust in AI-generated outputs within highly regulated environments. The conversation highlighted the importance of process-driven verification, the need to shift accountability to teams rather than individuals, and the strategic value of harness engineering for scalable, autonomous software delivery. Guidance was provided on selecting next-generation agentic platforms, refining organizational playbooks for AI trust, and iteratively improving harnesses to drive long-term productivity.

Key Actions

You should begin by evaluating your current AI and software development toolset, recognizing that legacy tools like Windsurf are limited to assistant roles and cannot support the transition to autonomous, agentic SDLC practices. Prioritize the adoption of agentic platforms such as Devin, Claude Code, or Codex, which offer robust safeguards and enterprise readiness, and explore partnerships with vendors and deploy engineers to accelerate platform onboarding. Invest in harness engineering by focusing on fixing systemic issues at the harness level rather than patching individual code outputs, ensuring that your automation engine improves with each iteration and supports parallel, scalable software production.

Develop and document clear playbooks for verifying AI-generated outputs, drawing analogies to existing human verification processes and disaster recovery planning to build organizational trust and resilience. Shift the accountability model from individuals to teams, particularly in non-safety-critical domains, to reduce single points of failure and foster a collaborative approach to risk management. Encourage iterative feedback and continuous improvement in both AI prompting and harness configuration, treating every error as an opportunity to strengthen your system and avoid recurring issues.

Stay informed on market trends, supply chain risks, and regulatory directives that may impact model selection and platform usage, adapting your strategy as needed to maintain compliance and operational continuity. By following these steps, you will position your organization to move beyond incremental AI productivity gains, embrace agentic SDLC maturity, and achieve scalable, trustworthy automation in software development.

Date: 21-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19352764
Buyer Region: EMEA
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: IT/Infrastructure and Operations - Other Role
Purpose: AI in the Modernisation of Legacy Technology - WR
Question Asked: What has been prioritised over the next financial year has been linked to technology health and tech debt of one of the older systems they have. They are interested in the role of AI in modernising this service, for example the use of gen AI tooling to do an analysis of the current technology stacks or agentic AI as part of the redesign. 

How can AI be used for the modernisation of legacy technology? Can they use AI to do an impact assessment of their current technology implementation?
Analyst Name: Erin Khoo
Discussion Summary: Thank you for your inquiry on Code Modernization and Tech Debt

Code and application modernization follows a three-stage process. Discover, Design and Delivery (execution). AI can play a role in each, but the Discovery stage also has a number of AI-adjacent technologies that are relevant.

Discovery:
Existing system snapshot; knowledge graphs, AST and vector dbs based on your existing architecture; Devsu, Mechanical Orchard
Redocumenting applications and integrations to understand data flows, business rules and processes; swimm.io
Agentic exploration and documentation; Claude code, Codex, OpenHands, Cursor etc
Reverse engineering system architecture; creating relational diagram representation optimal for AI ‘understanding’; mermaid.js, eraser.io
Codebase scanning tools to understand ‘legacy’ and code complexity to support strategy; CodeScene
Design:
Utilizing AI agents to accelerate the design of target application/system architecture knowing existing architecture and dependencies
Strangler fig pattern of progressively migrating/building one component at a time but using AI in the planning stage to define jobs to be done and priority
Embed your own standards, technical choices and security processes into AI systems so they build in the right direction to the target system architecture
Humans still heavily in the loop, complex system design choices not able to be masterfully done by ‘AI'
Acceptance criteria (AC) and scenario scoping with AI. You can complete discovery and have AI tools rewrite acceptance criteria and then execute a new build just with the insights gathered by discovery. Utilize AC as a fresh build based on known limitations and technical restrictions.
Delivery:
Use general purpose coding assistants as an accelerant to complex ‘brownfield’ aspects to code modernization and AI agent for more automated, boilerplate tasks they are excellent at e.g. building a frontend, integrations endpoints, documentation, testing new applications.
Automate the verification step by utilizing independent, code review or AC critiquing AI agents to surface bugs and edge cases.
Have Agentic software agents work on highly spec’ed Issues/tickets/requirements, have them execute work as a junior engineer would from agile planning tools
https://cursor.com/for/code-modernization
https://openhands.dev/whitepapers/modernize-legacy-systems-with-ai-agents
https://claude.com/solutions/code-modernization
https://devsu.com/
https://aws.amazon.com/transform/
https://www.moderne.ai/solutions/scale-openrewrite

Analyst Name: Joerg Fritsch
Discussion Summary: Immuta is a DSP (link to the Market Guide DSP below) that allows fine grained access rules for data lakes. Data Lakes it covers are foremost Databricks and Snowflake. But it covers also amazon redshift, google big query and the query accelerator starburst. 

To configure the access rules for these data lakes with business context in mind, Immuta leverages metadata about these data lakes from Alation.

Alation discovers data in data lakes and traditional databases. The connection between Alation and BigID is primarily designed to enrich metadata for existing catalogue entries in Alation!

Alation is primarily designed for structured data. BigID covers structured and unstructured data but generally does not push information about unstructured data into Alation.

None of the components is designed to improve search across unstructured data.

To improve search across unstructured data Glean is very popular.

Traditional document management platforms such as OpenText may have a play here.

Clients w medium amounts of data frequently rely on Microsoft Copliot _or_ , for larger volumes use a RAG architecture and the openAI API or an inhouse LLM (several options exist).

Summary:
- The discussion focused on AI governance, specifically in the context of generative AI usage within a large organization.
- Sameer inquired about implementing AI governance to manage the use of generative AI tools by 16,000 employees, expressing concerns about data security and the need for structured guidelines.
- Leigh introduced a tiered AI governance model with four layers, emphasizing the importance of understanding control points and making informed decisions.
- The first layer involves AI that does not require privileged data, suggesting the use of AI gateways or prompt proxies to manage access.
- The second layer addresses AI that can change systems of record or affect the physical world, requiring protection of both the prompt and action layers.
- The third layer focuses on AI that creates or runs code, necessitating containment within secure environments like containers or virtual machines.
- The fourth layer involves AI interacting with other AI, using a fine dining kitchen metaphor to illustrate the need for small, task-specific agents and secure communication.
- Leigh emphasized the importance of protecting prompts and using simple measures like regex filters to prevent malinformation.
- Sameer expressed interest in the governance model as a guide for future conversations and preemptive measures.
- Leigh advised focusing on AI-assisted software engineering, highlighting the benefits of pre-configured tools and system prompts for secure code generation.
- The conversation touched on the rapid advancements in AI coding tools, suggesting a push for more AI use in system design and configuration to reduce errors.
- Jacques mentioned the need to align with other workstreams and engagements to ensure consistency in AI governance approaches.
- The session concluded with an invitation for further questions and a reminder of the support available from Gartner for ongoing research and implementation.

Cost Structure	Consumption-based, usage optimization through autoscaling, reserved instances, and other levers	Fixed monthly pricing (e.g., Windows 365) offering cost predictability
Innovation Focus	Broad portfolio expansion with continuous innovation; aggressive capacity expansion for AI workloads, though facing competitive challenges	Focus on enterprise transformation and hybrid cloud; strong integration with AI initiatives (powered by OpenAI and partnerships)
Partner Ecosystem	Mature, competency-based AWS Partner Network with high specialization	Extensive partner network with a focus on validated hardware partnerships and deep enterprise integration
Global Infrastructure	Extensive, globally distributed regions and zones enabling high scalability and diverse workloads	Strong global reach with strategic focus on regions where hybrid and regulated cloud operations are critical

Date: 17-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19460132
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Manufacturing
Buyer Role: Chief Compliance or Ethics Officer
Purpose: AI Workflow - Vendor and Use Cases
Question Asked: From the compliance view: how can we do more with less?

Analyst Name: James Crocker
Discussion Summary: Thank you for your questions. In brief, the questions I received were:
How can we use AI to do more with less (such as in COI disclosure), given that we have recently lost an FTE and will not be Abel to backfill?
What are the top use cases and vendors for AI in compliance?

Identifying AI Use Cases

To identify AI use cases, conduct a structured review of your department’s workflows to identify where the greatest friction exists (following the model of “How to Map Legal Workflows to AI Use Cases” below). 
Use a workload analysis to understand where your department spends the most time and resources currently.
Identify “problem statements” within resource-intensive workflows to clarify the pain point and highlight the underlying structure of the tas
Align potential AI capabilities to problem statements. Different types of AI have different types of capabilities - see the research note below “When Not to Use Generative AI” for a list of AI capabilities and aligned types of AI system.
Use this list of capabilities to start identifying AI systems, either through experimentation with existing enterprise AI tools or through working with IT to identify vendors (see below).

To apply this to Conflicts of Interest:
Map out your current COI review process.
Speak with staff to identify current points of friction
Frame problem statements regarding the review process
Identify whether problems can be resolved with process changes
Identify relevant AI capabilities to address remaining issues
Experiment with enterprise AI systems for review at key points

You will find examples of some of the AI use cases we have observed below in our “Legal and Compliance AI Use Case Library”, but we are continuously hearing about more ways that compliance functions are using it.

Technological Pathways to Implementing AI in Compliance
There are several different ways that we identify compliance leaders implementing AI which fit into roughly four different categories:
Local/IT development of an AI system: This occurs when either IT or a member of the compliance function with technical abilities identifies a need and develops an application from scratch, usually built on top of a foundation model from one of the large AI organizations like OpenAI or Anthropic. This is relatively rare and occurred more in 2023 and 2024 before vendors solutions came onto the market.
Compliance use of a general-purpose enterprise AI system: This could include use of an enterprise subscription to a chatbot like ChatGPT or use of a simple agent builder like CoPilot Studio or Agent Builder. These allow compliance to develop unique use cases for compliance using existing tools that associates may already have access to. Examples here could be a simple agent used to review forms to identify non-compliance against a standard. Compliance can experiment with these systems without the AI of IT.
Task-specific enterprise AI platforms: These are platforms, typically purchased by IT, that fulfill a specific task that can be used broadly across other functions. For example, Conversational AI Platforms are platforms which facilitate the development of chatbots within an enterprise. These can serve as the technological foundation for customer service chatbots, HR chatbots, but also Compliance Policy chatbots. Compliance leaders should reach out to IT to identify platforms already in place that can provide required capabilities based on identified AI use cases.
Traditional compliance vendors integrating AI into solutions: We’re seeing many compliance vendors, for instance, GRC providers, regulatory intelligence tools and third-party risk management tools integrate AI into their solutions. Ask your vendors about new capabilities they are adding and compare them to identified use cases to see if there are new capabilities in your existing solutions that could provide greater value to the department.
New, AI-native compl

Date: 12-May-26
Reference Number: 19495171
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: Divisional Technology Leader
Purpose: Anthropic Claude Code
Question Asked: College Ave would like to speak with C.A Swan regarding his recent article, "How to Adopt Anthropic's Claude Code at Scale?". Key questions include:
-	If we’re not using it at a production level but more for experimentation, what are must haves that we need to adopt from this article?
-	If we’re on virtual machines and only allowing generic documents (no PII or confidential info) to be put into Claude Code, what “shortcuts” can we take? Do we need to create the harness?
Analyst Name: C.A. Swan
Discussion Summary: Meeting Summary

We discussed the governance and implementation strategy for piloting Claude Code within your organization, focusing on balancing its advanced capabilities with the need for robust oversight compared to alternatives like Codex. You sought guidance on structuring a harness engineering approach, establishing context engineering as the foundation, and deploying small cross-functional teams to manage the pilot effectively. We recommended prioritizing the recruitment of a specialized harness engineer, implementing strong context and security controls before scaling, and adopting iterative, factory-style workflows to maximize both productivity and governance throughout the pilot.

Key Actions

You should begin by recruiting or designating a highly skilled harness engineer—the “unicorn” role—who will architect and maintain the governance platform that sits between Claude Code and your end users. This harness must be capable of model routing, context and prompt management, tool integration, and enforcement of security and linting standards, serving as the central layer for control and scalability across multiple AI platforms. Start your implementation with rigorous context engineering: document all relevant methodologies, tooling standards, and industry-specific processes, and ensure that all confidential or personally identifiable information is thoroughly scrubbed from documentation before agents are granted access. This foundational work in context management is essential before introducing additional security or back-pressure controls.

Deploy the pilot using small, cross-functional teams (2–5 members each) that cover all necessary roles—business analysis, quality assurance, engineering, and product management. These teams should be responsible for creating detailed specifications (“CAD files”) that feed into the harness, with all outputs evaluated and iterated through human review and adjustment of instructions or configurations, rather than direct artifact modification. Prepare for an initial dip in productivity as the organization adapts to the new workflows, understanding that several iterations may be needed to refine the harness and optimize team performance.

Adopt a learning strategy that leverages public Slack channels for agent interactions, allowing only channel owners to issue instructions while others observe and learn prompt engineering skills by osmosis. This transparent approach accelerates knowledge transfer and helps standardize best practices across teams. As you mature, evolve toward a “factory model” for your software lifecycle, automating transitions between research, planning, implementation, and verification stages, with clear swim lanes and agent-driven quality gates. Ensure that agents are empowered to reject incomplete or unclear inputs, sending them back for human clarification to maintain high standards of output. By following this structured, governance-first approach, you will maximize the strategic value of Claude Code while maintaining compliance, security, and operational excellence throughout your AI adoption journey.

Analyst Name: Adam Preset
Discussion Summary: The client was advised that Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot rely exclusively on Microsoft’s own Azure Speech-to-Text engine for meeting transcription and Copilot grounding, and this engine cannot be replaced or redirected to a third-party provider. The response clarified that while transcription settings, language selection, and compliance controls are configurable within Microsoft 365, the core engine and Copilot’s use of transcripts are fixed for security, compliance, and integration reasons. Alternatives such as third-party meeting assistants (e.g., Otter.ai, Fireflies.ai) and offline transcription using tools like OpenAI Whisper were presented, but each introduces trade-offs related to data sovereignty, privacy, operational effort, and integration. The client was cautioned that third-party and offline solutions cannot feed improved transcripts back into Copilot, and that operational complexity and compliance risks must be carefully evaluated. The recommendation was to focus on optimizing native Teams/Copilot transcription through meeting best practices and to pilot any alternative solution before broader adoption. This guidance provided a reality check on what is and is not possible with Copilot, and outlined practical alternatives for organizations with advanced transcription or sovereignty needs.
The client received a clear reality check on the technical limitations of Microsoft 365 Copilot transcription and actionable guidance on practical alternatives, enabling informed decisions about AI meeting assistant strategies and compliance. #value #AIvalue

Date: 15-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19344795
Buyer Region: EMEA
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: CIO or Head of Technology
Purpose: Claude Code and GitHub
Question Asked: Claude Code and GitHub:
We discussed the HIQA interest to explore capabilities of ‘Claude Code’ and ‘GitHub’ to enhance development capabilities in the team. We agreed the following:
•	Set-up introductory  Analyst Call(s) to explore capabilities of ‘Claude Code’ and ‘GitHub’… this may be one or two calls depending on the Analysts FB.
Analyst Name: C.A. Swan
Discussion Summary: Meeting Summary

We discussed how to accelerate Claude Code and agentic coding adoption inside an innovation hub sandbox before scaling it across the broader engineering organization as part of a second five-year digital and AI transformation strategy. We worked through the paradigm shift from handcrafted software development to a manufacturing model in which agents produce software inside a harness, and we covered why fixing the source of agent mistakes matters more than fixing individual outputs. We also walked through the four-factory model (research, plan, build, verification), the composition of the harness engineering team, and why throughput must be balanced across all four factories.

Key Actions

Stand up a small sandbox inside the innovation hub before any mainstream rollout. Claude Code is best-of-breed but ships as a glass cannon with most safety defaults off, so blast radius must be controlled through whitelisted tool access, sandboxed execution and incremental expansion of permissions. Treat the first project as a learning vehicle, not a production deliverable, and accept that productivity will dip before it climbs in a hockey-stick pattern.

Form a dedicated harness engineering team of four to five people drawn from existing platform-oriented engineers. Look for platform tooling experience, an obsession with automation, fluency with MCP, prompt and context engineering, integration experience (especially against tools like Jira) and at least one person with a security background. Hands-on exposure to Claude Code, Codex or Cursor is a strong plus. This team builds and maintains the harness; it does not write feature code.

Separate harness engineering from implementation and enforce a tight feedback loop between them. Implementation engineers must resist the urge to whittle away at agent output by hand. When the agent produces wrong output, the answer is to fix the instructions or the harness and rerun, not to edit the artifact. Apply this same rule in production: when a bug is found, delete the branch, fix the root cause in the spec or harness, and regenerate. Treat genuine change requests as new micro-specs fed into the printer rather than edits to existing code.

Push as much verification as possible into the harness as deterministic back pressure. Test coverage thresholds, linting, static analysis, latency budgets, security checks and quality gates should run before the agent declares completion, so the agent self-corrects rather than handing low-quality work to humans. Human review should be the smallest possible step at the end, not the primary quality mechanism.

Plan for four factories, not one. The build factory alone will not deliver throughput if the research factory (idea to PRD), plan factory (PRD to work items) and verification factory (software to validated release) are not equally invested in. Each factory runs agents only, takes input through a chat-style interface (Slack, Teams, Discord), and iterates with humans outside the factory walls. Balance capacity across all four to avoid creating new bottlenecks upstream or downstream of the build phase.

Get comfortable trusting black-box production. The operating model resembles outsourced manufacturing: send in clear requirements, accept samples, approve or reject, and trust the factory to deliver against the spec without inspecting every internal step.
