- Melanie emphasized reviewing AI contract terms at least annually, as the landscape changes rapidly and vendor maturity is still developing.

Date: 20-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19346531
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: Software Engineering - Other Role
Purpose: AI in SDLC
Question Asked: Raji is the Head of Corporate Technology at First Citizens Bank. The client would like to understand the impact of AI in SDLC, we are requesting this call be aligned to C.A. Swan. 

Questions: 
-What are the new trends for AI in SDLC in the last 6 months?
-How is AI in impacting the SDLC process? 
-What tools are there to apply AI into SDLC process?
-What will the future of the developer role look like?
-How should a CIO incorporate AI into SDLC for their development team?
Analyst Name: C.A. Swan
Discussion Summary: Meeting Summary

We discussed how to approach agentic SDLC adoption from a pre-manual starting point, where no AI is in use today and the objective is to reimagine the delivery process rather than bolt AI onto individual SDLC tasks. We covered the manufacturing model of AI software delivery (specifications feed a coding harness that produces the artifact, and when output is wrong the harness is fixed rather than the artifact), the split between the vendor-provided harness platform and the enterprise-built harness inputs, and the organizational division of labor where a platform team engineers the harness while smaller, blended application teams produce specifications and consume it. The bulk of the guidance focused on the talent gap: harness engineering is a new discipline with no true experts yet, upskilling traditional developers rarely works, and identifying a small group of technically savvy, AI-curious engineers is the first and most decisive step before tool selection or rollout.

Key Actions

Identify the engineers who will lead harness engineering before selecting platforms, writing specifications or committing to a vendor. This is the single most important decision in the program. Look for technically strong engineers who are already experimenting with AI coding agents on their own time, who engage with limitations by proposing workarounds rather than by declaring the work impossible, and who understand both the target systems and the agent tooling well enough to bridge the two. Avoid broad upskilling programs intended to turn traditional developers into harness engineers; the results are weak. If the in-house talent is not available, contract deployed harness engineers from firms that offer them, but require them to work hands-on alongside internal engineers from day one so that institutional capability remains after the contract ends.

Separate the harness platform from the harness inputs and assign clear ownership for each. The platform team owns platform selection (Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot or equivalent) and the construction of the enterprise harness layer: context files, enforcement hooks, verification gates and managed settings. Smaller application teams, blended across engineering, QA and product, own specification files and consume the released harness. When the application team sees recurring mistakes in agent output, they must escalate to the platform team to patch the harness rather than repeatedly patching the artifact. Fixing artifacts teaches the harness nothing; fixing the harness compounds.

Apply harness engineering across every SDLC phase, not only implementation. The most common failure pattern is concentrating investment on coding while leaving planning, research and verification as human bottlenecks. Shrinking the human in implementation while leaving the human large in planning produces no throughput gain because bottlenecks shift rather than close. Use the harness in the planning phase to interrogate requirements, identify gaps, ambiguities and unanswered questions, and refuse to begin work until they are closed. Then use the harness in implementation to re-verify the same work units before coding begins and to enforce context and back-pressure rules during coding.

Treat every agent failure as a signal to improve the harness. Feed organizational rules (test coverage thresholds, code complexity limits, architectural constraints) into enforcement hooks so the harness blocks violations during generation rather than catching them post-merge. Expand context coverage whenever the agent makes an assumption, and expand back pressure whenever output escapes the rules the organization already requires. The best harness engineers use the harness itself to improve the harness.

Move beyond reach and views. Require platforms to calculate Earned Media Value (EMV) and offer bi-directional CRM integrations (e.g., Salesforce) to connect social engagement directly to revenue and Customer Lifetime Value (LTV).
3.	Customer Care & Unified Inbox
Monitoring sentiment is essential, but actionable response is critical. Add requirements for a Unified Inbox with automated case routing, chatbot handoffs, and integration with customer service teams to efficiently resolve complaints—especially those surfaced from dark ads or viral posts.
4.	Publishing Governance & Brand Compliance
Scheduling across platforms is foundational. Enhance this with multi-step, conditional approval workflows (e.g., “If a post contains X, route to Legal”) and automated AI-driven brand compliance scoring.
5.	Additional Enhancements
o	Competitor Benchmarking: Direct share-of-voice and sentiment comparison dashboards
o	Influencer & KOL Tracking: Monitor influential voices and their impact
o	Integration Capabilities: Ensure API support for BI and CRM tools
o	Data Privacy & Compliance: Confirm GDPR/CCPA compliance
o	Automated Reporting: Scheduled, branded report generation
o	Language & Region Coverage: Validate global support
o	Bot/Spam Detection: Filter out non-human content
o	Visual Content Moderation: Automated flagging of inappropriate content

Everyday AI: Broadly accessible AI for general productivity across the workforce.
Role-Specific AI: Targeted solutions for high-value roles/functions, requiring deeper workflow integration and measurable ROI.
No-Code/Low-Code AI: Tools enabling power users and domain experts to build/configure AI solutions without developer resources, extending AI’s reach while maintaining governance.
Custom AI Applications: Bespoke, business-critical solutions where off-the-shelf tools are inadequate, demanding higher investment and oversight.

This model clarifies the intended audience, expected outcomes, and governance needs for each AI initiative, supporting more intentional and effective adoption.
We discussed the importance of extracting use cases directly from business users and referenced toolkits to facilitate this process. Comparative guidance on leading AI platforms was provided, along with deployment recommendations for Anthropic Claude. Specifically, we advise a phased, intentional rollout of Claude and similar platforms, with rigorous governance and ROI validation. Avoid broad, indiscriminate deployment—these technologies, while promising, are still maturing and should not be treated as fully established ecosystems.
Relevant research and practical toolkits were shared to support your strategy and upcoming meetings. These resources include in-depth comparisons, deployment guides, and frameworks for identifying high-value use cases.

We provided the client with a structured four-layer model for enterprise AI adoption, enabling them to align AI initiatives with business needs, governance, and investment levels. Additionally, we advised on phased, intentional deployment of emerging AI platforms like Anthropic Claude to maximize ROI and manage risk. #value #AIvalue
